newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori returns to offensive.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori returns to offensive.

text.p: After three weeks of unusually low-profile activity, Peru's President Alberto Fujimori has shaken off the dark cloud that has hung over him since Marxist rebels seized the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and returned to the offensive.

Shaking hands and striding out purposefully, the natural campaigner, who has won two landslide election victories, took to the streets earlier this week in a drive to win back the propaganda initiative from Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas still holding 74 hostages.
"He had to get back out there. The MRTA had been winning the propaganda war hands down," said one diplomat, who asked not to be named.
In typical flamboyant style, Fujimori made whistle-stop tours of shantytowns in the capital on Tuesday and Wednesday, lambasting the MRTA as terrorists and pledging a peaceful end to the siege.
In the central Lima shantytown of Villa Rica a relaxed Fujimori, wearing jeans and a casual white shirt, perched on the roof of his car and worked the crowd.
"Do you think we should maintain a firm position against the terrorists?" he asked. "Yes!" people yelled back, encouraged by Fujimori aides.
"Should the government set free the leaders of the MRTA?" he continued. "No!" the people replied as they waved Peruvian and Japanese flags distributed moments before Fujimori's "surprise" arrival.
The MRTA guerrillas are demanding the release of jailed comrades.

Fujimori's performance was a sharp contrast to his behaviour before Tuesday. Fujimori, 58, had spoken only twice in public since about 20 heavily-armed guerrillas stormed a Christmas cocktail party at the residence and took more than 500 guests hostage.

Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, refused to negotiate directly with the rebels, flatly rejected their demands and bunkered down with close advisers. On his rare public appearances, he looked grim and preoccupied.
"He has this tendency to go into his shell whenever there's a crisis," said opposition congressman Carlos Chipoco.
But the silent strategy appeared to damage Fujimori. He found himself on the wrong end of a propaganda war launched by an enemy he claimed to have virtually wiped out.
From crude banners to the latest internet technology, the Marxist rebels have resisted Fujimori's attempts to keep them quiet and play down the crisis.
On New Year's Eve a group of journalists evaded lax police security to enter the residence and hold an impromptu news conference with Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, leader of the guerrillas.
Government sources said Fujimori was enraged by the rebels' propaganda coup. "They (the MRTA) took the initiative and made a mockery of him," one source said.
"Normally he never stops, constantly visiting shantytowns and the interior. That's why these last few weeks have been so different. He's been very reserved," another palace source said.
By returning to his customary style of meeting the people, Fujimori is trying to turn the tables and prove the hostage crisis is an isolated incident, analysts said.
"This ... return to the street is intended to show that life is going on as normal, that the crisis has not affected the country," said Carlos Reyna, chief political analyst at the DESCO think-tank.

But Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is one of the remaining hostages -- more than 400 have been released over the last three weeks -- may find it difficult to make the crisis go away until it has been resolved.
"He doesn't want to feel trapped in the Palace. But every time he goes out people will ask about the crisis. It's going to be tough to shake it off," Chipoco said.
